prompt.context: Heinz recently came up with the idea to double the volume of ketchup in a single-serve packet.
prompt.question: How should the CEO approach this idea and what should he do?

clarifying_info.q: How big is the market and what is Heinz's share?
clarifying_info.a: $500 million industry. Heinz has 60% of the market.

clarifying_info.q: Who are Heinz's customers and what do they care about?
clarifying_info.a: Heinz sells directly to large chains (e.g., McDonald's) and to food distributors (e.g., Sysco). Customers are entirely focused on keeping their costs low.

clarifying_info.q: How do end users actually consume the packets?
clarifying_info.a: Only 5% of customers use just 1 packet; 95% use 3–4 packets per sitting; usage maxes out at 16 packets per sitting.

clarifying_info.q: Is anyone else doing this? Will it be a competitive advantage?
clarifying_info.a: No competitor is currently doing this, but they would likely copy the idea if it proved successful. So this will not be a source of sustainable competitive advantage.

clarifying_info.q: What happens to revenue if the packet volume doubles?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue is expected to be mostly flat at 60% of $500M. Ketchup is sold by the ton, so any large increase in amount purchased would be mostly offset by volume discounts given to customers.

clarifying_info.q: What are the current cost economics?
clarifying_info.a: 20% margins, so production cost is $240M/year. Fixed costs are 50% of that ($120M) and are expected to be static. Variable costs: ketchup materials are 50% of VC (with ~0.3% savings, about $180K); packet raw materials are the other 50% of VC ($60M). Assume the current packet is a 2x2x2 cube, so volume = 8, surface area = 24.

framework: Assess revenue impact: will doubling packet size change total ketchup revenue, or will volume discounts offset any gains?
Assess cost impact: decompose production costs into fixed vs. variable, and within variable costs, isolate ketchup material costs vs. packet raw material costs
Perform geometry/math: calculate the surface area of the new larger packet vs. two old packets to quantify raw material savings
Assess competitive dynamics: will this be a lasting advantage or will competitors replicate it?
Assess feasibility and buy-in: are there switching costs, and can Heinz get customer buy-in given customers only care about their own costs staying low?
Form a recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: How does doubling the packet volume affect Heinz's revenue?
questions.guidance: Revenue is expected to remain mostly flat. Heinz has 60% of a $500M market (~$300M revenue). Ketchup is sold by the ton, so any increase in volume purchased would be largely offset by volume discounts. The candidate should conclude revenue is not the lever here and pivot attention to costs.

questions.prompt: Break down Heinz's cost structure. What is the key variable cost to analyze?
questions.guidance: Production cost = $240M/year (20% margins on ~$300M revenue implied, but casebook states $240M directly). Fixed costs = 50% of $240M = $120M (static). Variable costs = $120M total. Ketchup materials = 50% of VC = $60M; savings from the new design ~0.3% = ~$180K (immaterial). Packet raw materials = 50% of VC = $60M. The key insight: the packet raw material cost is where the significant savings opportunity lies.

math.setup: Total production cost = $240M. VC = 50% of $240M = $120M. Packet raw material VC = 50% of $120M = $60M.
math.answer: Packet raw materials cost $60M/year; ketchup material savings are negligible at ~$180K

questions.prompt: If the packet volume doubles, how does the surface area (and thus raw material cost) change? Assume cube geometry.
questions.guidance: Current packet is a cube with volume 8 and surface area 24. New packet has volume 16 (doubled). The cube root of 16 ≈ 2.52, so each side ≈ 2.52. New surface area = 2.52² × 6 ≈ 37.5. Two old packets would have surface area = 2 × 24 = 48. Savings = (48 – 37.5) / 48 ≈ 22%, roughly 25%. At $60M packet raw material cost, a 25% savings = $15M/year. This is the crux of the case.

math.setup: Old packet: side = 2 (cube, volume = 2³ = 8, surface area = 6 × 2² = 24). New packet: volume = 16, side = 16^(1/3) ≈ 2.52, surface area = 6 × 2.52² ≈ 37.5. Compare to two old packets (SA = 48).
steps: Old side = 2, SA_old = 6 × 4 = 24; two old packets SA = 48
Savings in SA = 48 – 37.5 = 10.5; savings % = 10.5/48 ≈ 22%, round to ~25%
math.answer: ~$15M/year savings in packet raw material costs

brainstorming.prompt: What conditions or factors should Heinz consider before proceeding with the double-packet idea?

categories.name: Customer acceptance
ideas: Customers (chains, distributors) only care about cost—Heinz must demonstrate cost neutrality or savings pass-through
End users consuming 3–4 packets anyway; a larger packet may reduce total packets used but that shifts savings to Heinz on materials
Need buy-in from large chains who may have contracts or equipment tied to current packet size

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: No competitor is doing this now, but success will be quickly replicated
Not a source of sustainable competitive advantage—purely an efficiency play
Should act before competitors can match, to capture first-mover cost savings

categories.name: Operational / switching costs
ideas: May require changes to production line or packaging equipment
Distributors and restaurants may need new dispensers or storage adjustments
Switching costs could erode the $15M savings if large capital investment required

categories.name: Revenue risks
ideas: If customers use fewer packets per sitting (e.g., the double packet replaces two), Heinz sells fewer packets and volume discounts may reduce revenue
Must model whether net unit revenue stays flat given ton-based pricing

categories.name: Implementation
ideas: Pilot with select chains before full rollout
Negotiate volume discount terms in advance
Assess whether raw material suppliers can scale packet material at same unit cost

recommendation: Heinz should proceed with the double-packet initiative primarily because it generates approximately $15M/year in packet raw material savings—a meaningful reduction against a $240M cost base
Revenue is expected to remain flat, so this is a cost-reduction play, not a revenue growth story
The idea does not create a lasting competitive advantage (competitors will copy), but it is still worth doing for the cost efficiency, provided switching costs are manageable
risks: Competitors quickly replicate, eroding any pricing advantage
Customer buy-in may be difficult if chains have equipment or operational constraints tied to current packet size
Switching costs (production retooling, new dispensers) could partially or fully offset the $15M savings
Revenue could dip if customers reduce total ketchup purchased per order
next_steps: Quantify switching costs: model capital investment needed for production line changes
Pilot with 1–2 large chain customers to validate acceptance and measure actual usage behavior change
Model the full P&L impact including any volume discount renegotiation
If pilot is successful and switching costs are low, roll out broadly before competitors can react
